rv.q: Bedlam started out back in 2013 by staging tiny-cast productions; here the director Eric Tucker returns triumphantly to that stripped-down technique.
What’s most instructive about Bedlam’s “Othello” is how it reveals the taut mastery of Shakespeare’s writing.
Ryan Quinn, one of the best Othellos I've ever seen, changes, somewhat ironically, to Cassio's mistress, Bianca, with a slight reveal of the shoulders and a lilt to his voice.
Tucker’s Othello is a bell-ringing winner and, to mix metaphors, a lengthy feather in Bedlam’s cap.
As an actor, Tucker has a great ability to deliver Shakespeare in a manner that sounds colloquial without sacrificing its poetry.
Like other Bedlam treatments of classic works, Othello has intriguing elements yet a sense of no one at the steering wheel.
Returning to their initial concept, this four-character version of Othello is good as far as it goes but demonstrates the limits of too abbreviated Shakespeare.
You don’t need bells and whistles to make great theater.
Bedlam’s stripped-to-the-bone staging of Othello proves that less can indeed be electrifyingly more, as four actors conjure a harrowing world with precision and nerve.
The play is the thing and it is the talent of these actors, and devotion to their craft, that creates this intriguing and satisfying “Othello.”
With so few actors playing so many roles, it's harder to identify with any one of them for very long, to put ourselves in their shoes and imagine how we too might become that monster.

cn.t: Bedlam's four-actor "Othello" earns mostly strong reviews for its raw intensity and seamless shape-shifting performances, though some find the bare-bones approach hard to follow without prior knowledge of the play.
